evidence_quotes.quote: Richer and larger localities in an urban area reduce provision of water and sewerage connections to the smaller houses in which poorer migrants would live to discourage the in-migration of these poorer migrants and deflect them to other localities.

A key aspect is that until the late 1980s and democratization, it was in principle “illegal” for localities to provide public infrastructure such as central sewer and water connections in either type of settlement. This gave an opportunistic excuse to deny or limit such provision.
In this paper, we focus on the notion of exclusion through lack of servicing, whether land is reported to have formal title or not and whether housing meets land-use regulations or not.

using a base set of locality characteristics (the Z’s), which are median household income in 1980, number of urban households in 1980, and the interaction between the two, with these variables all in logarithmic form.

We have Brazilian Population Census data for 1970, 1980, 1991 and 2000. These data contain a variety of information on housing size, tenure mode, and servicing of houses as well as basic socioeconomic information covering education, income, family structure, and migration.
We estimate the determinants of water provision to the types of houses in which the poor and low-educated primarily live (i.e., 1–3 room houses in 1991).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to central piped water connections (and descriptively/hedonically full servicing including central sewer connections) across Brazilian urban localities (Minimum Comparable Areas, MCAs), focusing on small 1-3 room houses typically occupied by low-income migrants.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision: 'include') because it examines municipal infrastructure governance, inter-jurisdictional strategic fiscal/service competition across localities within metropolitan areas, local socioeconomic political economy (median income, population size, and their interaction), and 1982 anti-military legislative vote shares in shaping water connection provision. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (narrow=no -> decision: 'exclude', E03). What the authors label 'exclusionary policy' is aggregate municipal under-provision of central water connections to small (1-3 room) houses itself, explicitly defined 'whether land is reported to have formal title or not and whether housing meets land-use regulations or not.' In Section 4, where water connection share is the outcome, the analyzed determinants are neighboring municipalities' servicing levels (Tiebout/Brueckner strategic interaction), locality median income, urban household count, income-by-size interaction, population density, and 1982 partisan vote share — none of which is a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, administrative discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). The pre-1988 illegality of servicing informal settlements and post-1988 constitutional democratization/slum-upgrading reforms are treated only as unanalysed macro-governance background ('working presumption' comparing 1991 and 2000 cross-sections), while local minimum lot-size zoning laws (>125 sq m) in Section 2.5 are compared only descriptively against migrant shares and untitled homeowner shares, never water or sanitation access. In Section 5, water connection coverage is the exposure predicting locality population growth rather than a service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains quantitative econometric analysis of Brazilian Population Census data (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000), 1982 election data, municipal survey data, and geological/insolation instrumental variables across 447 urban localities (351 predominantly urban MCAs in 55 multi-locality urban areas in the main regressions), using OLS, spatial autoregressive/error MLE, 2SLS, LIML, and district fixed-effects rent hedonic regressions. (End-of-paper table/figure pages 39-46, 48, and 50 are blank in the PDF text extraction, but all variables, sample definitions, methods, and key estimates are fully reported in the main text.)
criterion_notes.c4: Section 4 models a household water service access outcome: the share of small urban houses (1-3 rooms; counterfactual 7-9 room houses) connected to a central water network in 1991 and 2000 (alongside descriptive statistics on central water and central sewer 'full service' coverage in Section 2; Section 5 instead models locality household population growth and educational composition, and Appendix A models housing rents).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (urban localities / MCAs in Brazilian metropolitan areas aggregating census household records on 1-3 room and 7-9 room dwellings), exposures (Section 4: neighboring localities' water servicing share, locality income, size, income-size interaction, density, and 1982 partisan vote share; Section 5: 1991 share of small houses with central water connections), outcomes (Section 4: central water connection share; Section 5: 1991-2000 household growth overall and by education), and econometric study design.

study_design: Observational quantitative econometric study (cross-sectional/lagged-covariate spatial strategic-interaction OLS and MLE regressions, 2SLS/LIML instrumental-variables locality growth regressions, and district fixed-effects hedonic rent regressions using 1970-2000 Brazilian Census MCA panel data)
population_and_sample: Brazilian urban localities (Minimum Comparable Areas, MCAs, aggregating split municipalities) from 1970-2000 Census data (447 MCAs in 123 urban areas overall; primary regression sample of 351 predominantly urban MCAs in 55 multi-locality urban areas, plus 1980 rental dwellings across 56 districts in Sao Paulo and 24 districts in Rio de Janeiro)
exposure: Section 4 (service-determination models): weighted average of competing localities' small-house central water connection rates in the same urban area (strategic interaction), locality log median household income, log urban household count, income-by-size interaction, population density, and 1982 anti-military legislative vote share (with pre-1988 dictatorship vs. post-1988 democratization as unmodeled macro background); Section 5 (growth models): 1991 share of small (1-3 room) houses with a central water connection
outcome: Section 4: share of small urban houses (1-3 rooms; counterfactual 7-9 rooms) with a central water connection in 1991 and 2000 (plus descriptive water and central sewer full-service rates); Section 5: 1991-2000 locality urban household growth overall and by household-head education; Appendix A: 1980 rental prices
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification of Criterion 2 (whereas under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 it would be included). Although the paper empirically models household central water connection rates for small (1-3 room) urban houses in Brazil (Section 4), what the authors term 'exclusionary policy' is municipal infrastructure under-provision itself, explicitly defined regardless of formal land title or compliance with land-use regulations. The empirical determinants of water connection coverage tested in Section 4 are inter-municipal Tiebout/Brueckner strategic competition (other localities' water coverage), locality median income, locality size, their interaction, population density, and 1982 anti-military vote shares — not a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, rule-application discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Pre-1988 legal restrictions on servicing informal settlements vs. post-1988 democratization serve only as unanalysed macro-governance background, local minimum lot-size zoning laws (Section 2.5) are not linked to water/sanitation access, and Section 5 treats water connection coverage as the exposure predicting city population growth rather than as the outcome.
